name: Umar Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Umar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at an iron ore mine, drilling the holes they pack with explosives. Fly in, fly out: two weeks on site, one week home. I drove a taxi for twenty-two years, then app rides, and when the app company started testing driverless cars in our city I thought, right, time to get ahead of this, so I came here at fifty-six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how is it going, honestly?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I'm still slow. My hole depths drift and the drill-and-blast engineer, a young woman called Tash, sends me notes every shift. But I like it. I ask the AI on my phone to explain things after every shift, like why the ground was so soft on bench four, and then I go back and ask Tash if it was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, so we all got worked up for nothing. Online I'd probably say it's a shame, because the tools could have done a lot of good if they'd been pushed further. At work I'd just shrug and get back on the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd feel a little let down. I moved my whole life out here partly because I thought the change was coming and I wanted to be standing in the right place. But it also means my job is safe till I retire, so I'm not going to complain too loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep getting better, aim to stop getting Tash's notes by the end of next year. I'd still use AI every day for learning the job, checking my payslip, planning my week home. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each swing, because I started late and the pension's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small pinch of disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How exactly do you use AI on the job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly as a patient teacher. I take a photo of my drill log and ask it what I might be doing wrong, then I ask Tash. Sometimes it's rubbish and she laughs at me, but more often than not it points me at the right thing, and at fifty-eight I'll take any teacher who doesn't sigh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your plans change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Nadia, my wife, would be pleased, because she never liked the fly-in life and would want me home by sixty-two or so. I'd probably agree.

S0.say: I'd say we got worked up for nothing, and online I'd say it's a shame the tools weren't pushed further. At work he'd shrug and go back to the rig.
S0.think: He'd feel slightly let down after moving his life to be in the right place for the change. Still, it would mean his job is safe until he retires.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and aims to stop getting corrections from the engineer by the end of next year. Keeps using AI daily to learn the job and saves a little each swing for his thin pension.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small pinch of disappointment.
S0.quote: At fifty-eight I'll take any teacher who doesn't sigh.
S0.fieldNote: Umar is the rare miner who's mildly disappointed that AI might fizzle. He moved into mining to get ahead of driverless cars, so he's already made one deliberate move. He uses AI as a learning partner and checks its answers with a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if it's done fairly. Workers should share in the gains, through the union and through retraining the company pays for. I'd say that loudly, because people on the left sometimes just say no to everything and I don't think that helps anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's my chance. The mine's already talking about a remote operations centre in the city where people run the drills from screens. Screens and AI are the one thing I'm actually ahead of the young ones on, funnily enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the remote operations trial the day it's announced. I'd use my week home to do an online course in automation basics, maybe two hundred dollars. And I'd push at the union meeting for a training agreement, so it's not only people like me who get through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. Like the first day on the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're junior and still learning the drill. Why would they pick you for the remote room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. Maybe they wouldn't. But I can sit in front of five screens without panicking, and I've seen experienced blokes who'd rather quit. I'd make the case and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev on night shift, who's been drilling thirty years and can't open an email. He's brilliant on the rig and he'd be lost in the remote room. I'd want the union to make sure there's a place for people like him, even if it's training the machines.

S1.say: I'd say this is good if it's fair, with workers sharing the gains through the union and company-paid retraining. He'd push back on people on the left who say no to everything.
S1.think: He sees steady change as his chance, especially the planned remote operations centre. Screens and AI are where he's ahead of younger workers.
S1.do: Volunteers for the remote operations trial the day it's announced and spends about two hundred dollars on an online automation course. Pushes the union for a training agreement that includes other workers.
S1.quote: Screens and AI are the one thing I'm actually ahead of the young ones on, funnily enough.
S1.fieldNote: His progressive views show up as wanting a fair share of change rather than stopping it. He's honest that being junior may count against him. His worry for Kev shows he thinks about people who won't adapt as easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to act right now: a payment for everyone, tax the companies that own the robots, and a say for workers. Two years is too fast for people to sort it out on their own. I'd say it everywhere, online and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my head start doesn't count for much here. If the AI can run the drill and the remote room by 2028, there's no job for a fifty-eight-year-old trainee who's good with screens. I left the taxi to dodge one robot and walked straight into a bigger one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd talk to Nadia about whether we pay off the last bit of the car and keep the rest as cash. I'd try for a role on the team setting up the automated drills, because someone has to teach them our ground, and I'd learn whatever I could on the AI side. If that doesn't happen within a year, I'd look at drawing my pension early and doing something small on the side, maybe helping older people in our street use their AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, because I've done this before, but my stomach's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nadia that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've got about five months saved, the house is nearly paid, and I'm not too proud to do anything. She'd say, you always have a plan. I'd say, yes, but this one has holes in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back from saying in public?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm actually a bit fascinated. In public I'd talk about protecting workers, and I mean it. But privately part of me wants to see what this thing can do, even while it's taking my job.

S2.say: I'd say the government must act now with a payment for everyone, taxes on robot-owning companies and a voice for workers. Two years is too fast for people to manage alone.
S2.think: He thinks his head start with technology counts for little if AGI runs both the drill and the remote room by 2028. He left taxi driving to dodge one robot and walked into a bigger one.
S2.do: Keeps savings as cash and tries for a role helping set up the automated drills. If nothing comes within a year, looks at drawing his pension early and helping neighbours use AI tools as a side income.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight stomach, but not frozen.
S2.quote: I left the taxi to dodge one robot and walked straight into a bigger one.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptable person feels the squeeze when there's only two years. He stays in planning mode, which keeps him at anxious rather than alarmed. He openly admits a fascination with the technology that he wouldn't say in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if governments get on with it. I'd push for the companies to fund retraining and a basic income trial, and I'd tell the young ones at the mine to learn the systems, not fight them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three. I think I could ride the changeover, because they'll need people who understand both the old drills and the new systems for a few years. I'd be one of the people who helps switch the lights off, and I'm fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get on the remote operations team, even as a junior. I'd do a proper certificate in automation over two years of week-offs. I'd keep saving, aiming for a year's worth by 2030, and plan to retire around sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ladder instead of a cliff. With two years I'd be grabbing at anything. With five I can climb down one step at a time: drill, then remote room, then helping with the switchover, then out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're fine helping switch the lights off. Do you mean that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. It's a bit sad to be the one training the thing that replaces you and your mates. But someone's going to do it, and I'd rather it was someone who cares about the blokes who are leaving.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if governments get moving, with companies funding retraining and a basic income trial. He'd tell young miners to learn the systems rather than fight them.
S3.think: At sixty-three by 2031, he thinks he could ride the changeover, because the mine would need people who know both old and new. He'd be one of those who help switch the lights off.
S3.do: Joins the remote operations team in the first year and studies for an automation certificate over two years of weeks off. Saves towards a year's cushion by 2030 and plans to retire around sixty-three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more interested than worried.
S3.quote: A ladder instead of a cliff.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the change into a sequence of steps he can manage. He accepts the sad role of training his replacements and frames it as care for his mates. His plan lines up neatly with a retirement around sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a decade, so there's no excuse. I'd push the union to plan now, and I'd talk about it at the mosque and with friends, because most people will wait until year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's good. I'd be sixty-eight and retired. I'd have a few years of interesting work in the switchover and then a quiet life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on drilling and get properly good, then move into the remote room when it opens. I'd help my son, who's an apprentice electrician, think about where the work will be. And I'd keep saving as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him robots need power, and power needs people for a good while yet. Get your ticket, then learn how the automated sites wire everything up. He already rolls his eyes when I send him AI articles, so I'd send fewer and buy him a coffee instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything here that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the gains get shared. If ten years ends with a few companies owning every mine and robot and the rest of us on scraps, that's not a technology problem, that's a politics problem. That's the bit I'd keep fighting.

S4.say: I'd say a decade of warning leaves no excuse, and he'd push the union to plan now. He'd raise it at the mosque and with friends, since most people will wait until year nine.
S4.think: Personally it's good news: he'd be retired at sixty-eight after a few interesting years in the switchover. Then he'd have a quiet life.
S4.do: Keeps drilling until he's properly good, then moves into the remote room when it opens. Helps his apprentice electrician son plan where the work will be and keeps saving as he is.
S4.quote: If ten years ends with a few companies owning every mine and robot and the rest of us on scraps, that's not a technology problem, that's a politics problem.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Umar is relaxed and almost eager. His worry moves to whether the gains will be shared, which fits his progressive outlook. He'd help his son plan but is trying not to overload him with articles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where my plans don't have time to work. What would help is a guaranteed income for people pushed out before pension age, and the companies paying their share for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people like me enjoy learning at this age. I do. Every week I find out something new about rock or software. I just want to be allowed to keep learning, not told I'm too old for the next thing.

headlineQuote: I just want to be allowed to keep learning, not told I'm too old for the next thing.
portrait: Umar Rahman is a fifty-eight-year-old former taxi driver who now runs a blast-hole drill at a fly-in, fly-out iron ore mine. He moved into mining at fifty-six to stay ahead of driverless cars, uses AI every day to learn the job, and wants the gains from automation shared fairly. He stays calm through the plateau and steady change, seeing the mine's planned remote operations room as his chance. Only AGI in two years makes him anxious, and with five or ten years he plans a step-by-step path into retirement while fighting for workers' share.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because it's the only picture in which his plans have no time to work.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for people pushed out before pension age, funded partly by the companies.
